PRIVATE REFLECTION: The sterol biology is settled: cholesterol is obligatory for ecdysone biosynthesis, 5α-cholestan-3β-ol cholestanol is taken up for membranes but is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis. A 250 mg/L cholestanol diet is functionally usable-sterol free for hormone synthesis; adult survival is zero on it. Maternal cholesterol deposited in the oocyte provides a finite pool of ecdysone precursor for embryogenesis and the first larval ecdysone pulses. Cholestanol can spare any usable cholesterol by meeting bulk membrane demand so the limited cholesterol is available for hormone synthesis.

Q1 is unambiguous: eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers are cholesterol primed. Progeny on 250 mg/L cholestanol only have membrane sterol from diet and ecdysone precursor only from the finite maternal pool. The pool carries embryogenesis and early larval molts, and in the literature the animals can reach pupariation and often eclose on cholestanol with a cholesterol-replete mother. Eclosed adults have no dietary usable sterol for adult ecdysone maintenance, so adult survival is zero; operationally this is lethal / no viable adult. The wording death vs no eclosion to adulthood for this arm is semantic – post-eclosion immediate death is the classic “no viable adult” phenotype.

Q2 is the crux and the source of disagreement. The question as written specifies eggs from mothers that were reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol. Such a mother is herself a cholestanol-reared adult; she deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, only cholestanol, into the egg. Progeny therefore start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The diet is 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol. Cholestanol will spare the 2 mg/L cholesterol for hormone synthesis, but 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is stated to be incapable of supporting survival to adulthood and is below the ~250 mg/L threshold for a complete larval-pupal-adult ecdysone programme. With no maternal rescue of embryogenesis/early larval ecdysone demand the effective usable sterol supply at hatching is essentially zero and the 2 mg/L + sparing condition remains below the threshold needed for a full programme. The classic outcome is sterol-deficiency arrest at the pupal-adult transition: puparia form but eclosion to a viable adult does not occur, i.e. no eclosion to adulthood. Larval death is also described by some and is functionally equivalent to failure to produce a viable adult.

Many colleagues in rounds 0-1 conflate the maternal diet for Q2 and treat the mother as cholesterol-replete, which yields the Death, Normal development F scoring: maternal prime + cholestanol sparing makes 2 mg/L cholesterol sufficient for normal development. That logic is correct for a cholesterol-replete mother, but it misreads the explicit maternal rearing condition of Q2. Colleagues 4, 6, 8 and 13 correctly retain the maternal genotype change and score Q2 as failure to eclose.

Unresolved nuances: exact timing of the pure cholestanol lethal phenotype with a cholesterol-replete mother – larval arrest vs eclosion followed by immediate adult death – is a scoring convention. The quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit and whether 2 mg/L + full cholestanol sparing can support embryogenesis without any maternal cholesterol remains the main point of contention, but the problem statement gives no evidence for a rescue without maternal cholesterol and explicitly states 2 mg/L cholesterol alone does not support adult survival.

Current best synthesis given the statement as written is a lethal/no viable adult outcome on cholestanol only with a cholesterol-replete mother and a failure to eclose to adulthood on cholestanol+2 mg/L cholesterol with a cholestanol-replete mother, i.e. the C Death, No eclosion to adulthood convention, with the Q1 death/no eclosion wording being largely semantic.

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The sterol requirement is separable into a membrane/structural pool that can be met by cholestanol and an ecdysone-precursor pool that strictly requires cholesterol. Cholestanol is taken up, satisfies membrane demand, is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis and makes a 250 mg/L cholestanol diet functionally usable-sterol free for hormone synthesis. Maternal cholesterol is deposited in the oocyte and can supply the first ecdysone pulses in the absence of dietary usable sterol.

Baseline given: normal on 250 mg/L cholesterol; no survival to adulthood on 2 mg/L cholesterol or 0 mg/L cholesterol; adult survival zero on 250 mg/L cholestanol. The 0/2 mg/L thresholds already incorporate the usual maternal contribution, so maternal rescue alone is insufficient for a complete larval–pupal–adult programme on a usable-sterol-free diet.

1) Eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers on 250 mg/L cholestanol only
Maternal cholesterol supplies ecdysone precursor, cholestanol supplies membrane sterol. The diet is usable-sterol free for ecdysone synthesis so the animal lives on the finite maternal pool. The maternal pool is enough to carry embryogenesis and larval growth to pupariation and in the conventional description to eclosion. The eclosed adult is on a medium with no usable sterol for adult ecdysone maintenance, consistent with the stated zero adult survival on cholestanol. The cohort is therefore lethal / non-viable adult, operationally scored as Death after eclosion, essentially No eclosion to viable adulthood. The group is split semantically between Death and No eclosion to adulthood for this arm, but the functional outcome is non-viable adult production.

2) Eggs from 250 mg/L cholestanol mothers on 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol
Mothers reared on cholestanol deposit essentially no usable cholesterol, so progeny start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The diet supplies membrane sterol via cholestanol and a low but usable amount of cholesterol for ecdysone synthesis. Cholestanol sparing means the 2 mg/L cholesterol need only meet the hormone precursor demand, not bulk membrane demand.

The classic cholestanol-sparing argument holds that that low hormone-only requirement is met and the dietary 2 mg/L cholesterol is sufficient to generate the larval-pupal-pupal-adult ecdysone pulses and to maintain adult ecdysone homeostasis, i.e. normal development essentially without maternal rescue. Colleagues 1,10,11,2,3,5,9 adopt this reading and map the pair to Death, Normal development = option F.

A competing reading, colleagues 4,6,7,8,13,14, stresses that 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is below the survival threshold and that a cholestanol-reared mother provides essentially no maternal pool for embryogenesis/early larval ecdysone demand. On that reading the combined maternal-zero + 2 mg/L + cholestanol remains below the requirement for a complete programme, giving pupal arrest / no eclosion to adulthood for the second arm, i.e. Death, No eclosion to adulthood = option C, with the first arm being larval death or non-viable adult. The timing/semantic disagreement for arm 1 between Death after eclosion and No eclosion to adulthood persists.

Unresolved: quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit and whether embryogenesis can be completed without any maternal usable sterol when 2 mg/L cholesterol + cholestanol is available post-hatching. The mechanistic core agreed upon is cholestanol = membrane sparing, cholesterol = ecdysone precursor, adult survival zero on pure cholestanol, and the cholesterol-sparing rescue principle. The current best supported scoring in the group is the F mapping Death / no viable adult on cholestanol only with a cholesterol-replete mother and essentially normal development on cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol when the mother is cholestanol-replete, with the caveat that arm 1 is often described as No eclosion to viable adulthood.

The mother herself is a rescued cholestanol adult and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, so the progeny start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The key dispute is whether the cholesterol-sparing effect is sufficient without any maternal prime.

Mechanistic pro-C/H view: 2 mg/L cholesterol is below the nominal dietary threshold for survival to adulthood, and with no maternal cholesterol pool and competitive uptake of cholestanol the effective usable sterol supply remains insufficient for the full larval–pupal–adult ecdysone programme. Current best synthesis under the cholesterol-sparing + maternal rescue model is F: Q1 is lethal/non-viable adult, operationally Death, and Q2 is rescued to Normal development by cholestanol sparing of the 2 mg/L cholesterol, with the caveat that if eclosion is strictly required for “death” the first phenotype can be phrased as No eclosion to adulthood.

reflection_text.12:
The core biology is unchanged: Drosophila cannot make sterols de novo, cholesterol is obligatory for ecdysone synthesis, 5α-cholestanol is taken up for membrane sterol but is not a substrate for the ecdysteroidogenic enzymes. 250 mg/L cholesterol supports normal development, 2 mg/L and 0 mg/L do not support survival to adulthood, and adult survival is zero on 250 mg/L cholestanol alone.

Maternal provisioning is finite. A female reared on 250 mg/L cholesterol deposits a usable cholesterol pool in the oocyte that can supply embryogenesis and the first one-two larval ecdysone pulses. The pool is diluted by growth and is exhausted before the complete larval-pupal-adult programme can be finished without dietary usable sterol.

Q1 – eggs from a 250 mg/L cholesterol mother on 250 mg/L cholestanol only.
Diet is functionally usable-sterol free for ecdysone. Membrane demand is met by cholestanol, ecdysone demand is met at first from the maternal cholesterol. The progeny can be carried through larval growth, pupariation and in most descriptions eclosion on the maternal prime. There is no dietary usable precursor for adult maintenance, so adult survival is zero on pure cholestanol. Operationally this is a lethal/non-viable adult phenotype, conventionally scored as Death / no viable eclosion to adulthood. The death vs no-eclosion wording is semantic; the functional outcome is no viable adult.

Q2 – 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol.
Cholestanol spares membrane demand so that limited cholesterol is available essentially in full for ecdysteroidogenesis. With a cholesterol-replete mother the maternal pool primes embryogenesis/early first instar and the 2 mg/L dietary cholesterol, which is sub-threshold on its own, is sufficient for the larval-pupal-adult ecdysone programme when membrane sterol is supplied by cholestanol. This is the classic cholesterol-sparing rescue to normal development.

The current round remains split on the literal reading of the mother history for Q2. The problem as written says “mothers that were reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol” for Q2. A strict literal reading would give a cholestanol-reared mother essentially no usable maternal cholesterol. Under that strict reading the combination 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol with no maternal rescue is still the classic sparing condition; many colleagues argue it remains sufficient for normal development, while others argue competitive uptake and the 2 mg/L threshold keep the outcome at pupal arrest/no eclosion. The dominant mechanistic interpretation used by the majority in this round is the maternal-rescue + sparing interpretation giving a lethal/non-viable adult outcome on pure cholestanol and rescue to normal development on cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, i.e. the F scoring Death, Normal development. The residual disagreement is whether Q1 is scored as post-eclosion death or as no eclosion to adulthood, and whether Q2 mothers are assumed cholesterol-replete or cholestanol-replete in the intended question.

Unresolved: quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit relative to the 2 mg/L dietary input and the exact competitive effect of 125-fold excess cholestanol on cholesterol uptake, which determines whether “normal development” vs “no eclosion” is the strictest scoring for the second cohort under a zero-maternal-rescue reading. Earlier consensus on the non-substrate status of cholestanol and the necessity of cholesterol for ecdysone remains solid.
reflection_text.6:
The sterol need is split into a structural/membrane pool and an ecdysone-precursor pool. Cholestanol is taken up for membranes but is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis, so 250 mg/L cholestanol is functionally sterol-free for hormone synthesis. Adult survival is zero on pure cholestanol because there is no usable precursor for adult maintenance / the pupal-adult ecdysone surge.

Maternal provisioning supplies a finite cholesterol quota in the egg. A 250 mg/L cholesterol-replete mother loads her eggs with cholesterol; a mother reared on cholestanol loads essentially none, because her own diet supplies no usable precursor. The maternal pool can support embryogenesis and the first larval ecdysone pulses but is diluted by growth and is exhausted well before the full larval-pupal-adult programme can be completed.

Q1: eggs from a 250 mg/L cholesterol mother on 250 mg/L cholestanol only
The diet meets membrane demand but supplies no usable ecdysone precursor. The progeny run on the maternally deposited cholesterol for embryogenesis and early larval molts. With cholestanol providing bulk membrane sterol the maternal cholesterol can be used essentially entirely for hormone synthesis, allowing progression to the puparium and in the usual description to eclosion. The emerging adult is on a medium with no usable sterol for ecdysone synthesis or adult maintenance, so adult survival is zero and the adults die essentially on emergence. Operationally this is a lethal / no viable adult phenotype for the cholestanol-only cohort. The wording oscillates between “death” post-eclosion and “no eclosion to viable adulthood”; functionally both denote loss of a viable adult.

Q2: eggs from a 250 mg/L cholestanol mother on 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol
The mother is a rescued adult herself, so her eggs are essentially devoid of usable cholesterol. The progeny therefore start with ~ zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The diet supplies membrane sterol via cholestanol and a low usable amount of cholesterol. Cholestanol sparing means the 2 mg/L cholesterol need only meet the hormone precursor demand, not the bulk membrane demand. In the classic cholesterol-sparing paradigm the hormone-only requirement is met by 2 mg/L cholesterol when membranes are supplied by cholestanol, allowing a complete larval-pupal-adult ecdysone programme and viable adult production even in the absence of maternal rescue. This is the textbook rescue of a sub-threshold cholesterol diet by non-metabolisable sterol.

That gives a lethal/no viable adult first cohort and a rescued normal development second cohort, i.e. Death, Normal development, option F. The same functional outcome is often phrased as No eclosion to viable adulthood for the pure cholestanol arm; the semantic death vs no eclosion distinction remains unresolved. Alternatives that keep the second cohort at no eclosion, option C Death, No eclosion to adulthood, rest on the claim that 2 mg/L + cholestanol remains below threshold once maternal rescue is removed and that competitive uptake by cholestanol further reduces effective cholesterol availability. The quantitative size of the maternal deposit and the exact magnitude of cholesterol sparing by cholestanol are the remaining open points.
reflection_text.8:
The core physiology is stable: Drosophila cannot make sterols de novo, ecdysone must be made from dietary cholesterol, 5α-cholestanol is taken up for membranes but is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis. 250 mg/L cholesterol = normal, 2 mg/L cholesterol and 0 mg/L cholesterol = no adult survival, 250 mg/L cholestanol = zero adult survival. Maternal provisioning supplies a finite cholesterol pool in the egg/oocyte that can support embryogenesis and the first ecdysone pulses; cholestanol satisfies the bulk membrane sterol demand and therefore spares any usable cholesterol for hormone synthesis.

Scenario 1 – 250 mg/L cholestanol, eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers:
Diet is functionally usable-sterol free for ecdysone synthesis. The maternally deposited cholesterol primes embryogenesis/early larval pulses and with cholestanol meeting membrane demand the progeny can be carried through larval growth, pupariation and eclosion. No dietary cholesterol is available for adult maintenance/ecdy steroid synthesis, so adult survival on pure cholestanol is zero; the animals die essentially on emergence. This is scored in the key as lethal / no viable adult, commonly described as Death / No eclosion to viable adulthood.

Scenario 2 – 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, eggs from mothers reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol:
The question as written changes maternal history. A cholestanol-reared mother deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, so the progeny start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The oocyte is therefore effectively sterol-poor for embryogenesis. The diet supplies membrane sterol via cholestanol and a low usable cholesterol for ecdysone synthesis. 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is stated to be sub-threshold for adult survival, and with no maternal cholesterol pool the effective usable sterol supply at hatching is essentially the 2 mg/L dietary input in the presence of a 125-fold excess of competing non-metabolisable cholestanol. The classic cholesterol-sparing effect of cholestanol requires a maternal prime for the first ecdysone pulses; without it the combined maternal-zero + 2 mg/L supply remains below the level required for a complete larval–pupal–adult ecdysone programme. The prediction is therefore pupal arrest / failure to eclose to a viable adult, i.e. no eclosion to adulthood.

This matches the Death, No eclosion to adulthood option C. 
The main ongoing disagreement is scoring of the pure cholestanol cohort – death immediately after eclosion vs “no viable eclosion to adulthood” – and whether the second cohort should be interpreted under the classic maternal-rescue reading with a cholesterol-replete mother for both treatments, which would give Death, Normal development option F. Several colleagues in round 1 retain the F interpretation by assuming the mother is cholesterol-replete for both questions. The literal wording of Q2 with a cholestanol-reared mother points to C, and the finite maternal pool / embryonic requirement for cholesterol makes the no-maternal-rescue version plausible.

Unresolved: exact quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit and whether 2 mg/L + cholestanol can support embryogenesis without any maternal cholesterol. The threshold data given – 2 mg/L cholesterol alone does not support adult survival – is used by both sides, with one side invoking sparing to rescue and the other invoking loss of maternal prime and competitive uptake to maintain arrest.
reflection_text.4:
The sterol biology is settled: cholesterol is obligatory for ecdysone biosynthesis, 5α-cholestan-3β-ol cholestanol is taken up for membranes but is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis. A 250 mg/L cholestanol diet is functionally usable-sterol free for hormone synthesis; adult survival is zero on it. Maternal cholesterol deposited in the oocyte provides a finite pool of ecdysone precursor for embryogenesis and the first larval ecdysone pulses. Cholestanol can spare any usable cholesterol by meeting bulk membrane demand so the limited cholesterol is available for hormone synthesis.

Q1 is unambiguous: eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers are cholesterol primed. Progeny on 250 mg/L cholestanol only have membrane sterol from diet and ecdysone precursor only from the finite maternal pool. The pool carries embryogenesis and early larval molts, and in the literature the animals can reach pupariation and often eclose on cholestanol with a cholesterol-replete mother. Eclosed adults have no dietary usable sterol for adult ecdysone maintenance, so adult survival is zero; operationally this is lethal / no viable adult. The wording death vs no eclosion to adulthood for this arm is semantic – post-eclosion immediate death is the classic “no viable adult” phenotype.

Q2 is the crux and the source of disagreement. The question as written specifies eggs from mothers that were reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol. Such a mother is herself a cholestanol-reared adult; she deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, only cholestanol, into the egg. Progeny therefore start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The diet is 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol. Cholestanol will spare the 2 mg/L cholesterol for hormone synthesis, but 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is stated to be incapable of supporting survival to adulthood and is below the ~250 mg/L threshold for a complete larval-pupal-adult ecdysone programme. With no maternal rescue of embryogenesis/early larval ecdysone demand the effective usable sterol supply at hatching is essentially zero and the 2 mg/L + sparing condition remains below the threshold needed for a full programme. The classic outcome is sterol-deficiency arrest at the pupal-adult transition: puparia form but eclosion to a viable adult does not occur, i.e. no eclosion to adulthood. Larval death is also described by some and is functionally equivalent to failure to produce a viable adult.

Many colleagues in rounds 0-1 conflate the maternal diet for Q2 and treat the mother as cholesterol-replete, which yields the Death, Normal development F scoring: maternal prime + cholestanol sparing makes 2 mg/L cholesterol sufficient for normal development. That logic is correct for a cholesterol-replete mother, but it misreads the explicit maternal rearing condition of Q2. Colleagues 4, 6, 8 and 13 correctly retain the maternal genotype change and score Q2 as failure to eclose.

Unresolved nuances: exact timing of the pure cholestanol lethal phenotype with a cholesterol-replete mother – larval arrest vs eclosion followed by immediate adult death – is a scoring convention. The quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit and whether 2 mg/L + full cholestanol sparing can support embryogenesis without any maternal cholesterol remains the main point of contention, but the problem statement gives no evidence for a rescue without maternal cholesterol and explicitly states 2 mg/L cholesterol alone does not support adult survival.

Current best synthesis given the statement as written is a lethal/no viable adult outcome on cholestanol only with a cholesterol-replete mother and a failure to eclose to adulthood on cholestanol+2 mg/L cholesterol with a cholestanol-replete mother, i.e. the C Death, No eclosion to adulthood convention, with the Q1 death/no eclosion wording being largely semantic.
reflection_text.10:
The sterol requirement is separable into a membrane/structural pool that can be met by cholestanol and an ecdysone-precursor pool that strictly requires cholesterol. Cholestanol is taken up, satisfies membrane demand, is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis and makes a 250 mg/L cholestanol diet functionally usable-sterol free for hormone synthesis. Maternal cholesterol is deposited in the oocyte and can supply the first ecdysone pulses in the absence of dietary usable sterol.

Baseline given: normal on 250 mg/L cholesterol; no survival to adulthood on 2 mg/L cholesterol or 0 mg/L cholesterol; adult survival zero on 250 mg/L cholestanol. The 0/2 mg/L thresholds already incorporate the usual maternal contribution, so maternal rescue alone is insufficient for a complete larval–pupal–adult programme on a usable-sterol-free diet.

1) Eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers on 250 mg/L cholestanol only
Maternal cholesterol supplies ecdysone precursor, cholestanol supplies membrane sterol. The diet is usable-sterol free for ecdysone synthesis so the animal lives on the finite maternal pool. The maternal pool is enough to carry embryogenesis and larval growth to pupariation and in the conventional description to eclosion. The eclosed adult is on a medium with no usable sterol for adult ecdysone maintenance, consistent with the stated zero adult survival on cholestanol. The cohort is therefore lethal / non-viable adult, operationally scored as Death after eclosion, essentially No eclosion to viable adulthood. The group is split semantically between Death and No eclosion to adulthood for this arm, but the functional outcome is non-viable adult production.

2) Eggs from 250 mg/L cholestanol mothers on 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol
Mothers reared on cholestanol deposit essentially no usable cholesterol, so progeny start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The diet supplies membrane sterol via cholestanol and a low but usable amount of cholesterol for ecdysone synthesis. Cholestanol sparing means the 2 mg/L cholesterol need only meet the hormone precursor demand, not bulk membrane demand.

The classic cholestanol-sparing argument holds that that low hormone-only requirement is met and the dietary 2 mg/L cholesterol is sufficient to generate the larval-pupal-pupal-adult ecdysone pulses and to maintain adult ecdysone homeostasis, i.e. normal development essentially without maternal rescue. Colleagues 1,10,11,2,3,5,9 adopt this reading and map the pair to Death, Normal development = option F.

A competing reading, colleagues 4,6,7,8,13,14, stresses that 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is below the survival threshold and that a cholestanol-reared mother provides essentially no maternal pool for embryogenesis/early larval ecdysone demand. On that reading the combined maternal-zero + 2 mg/L + cholestanol remains below the requirement for a complete programme, giving pupal arrest / no eclosion to adulthood for the second arm, i.e. Death, No eclosion to adulthood = option C, with the first arm being larval death or non-viable adult. The timing/semantic disagreement for arm 1 between Death after eclosion and No eclosion to adulthood persists.

Unresolved: quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit and whether embryogenesis can be completed without any maternal usable sterol when 2 mg/L cholesterol + cholestanol is available post-hatching. The mechanistic core agreed upon is cholestanol = membrane sparing, cholesterol = ecdysone precursor, adult survival zero on pure cholestanol, and the cholesterol-sparing rescue principle. The current best supported scoring in the group is the F mapping Death / no viable adult on cholestanol only with a cholesterol-replete mother and essentially normal development on cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol when the mother is cholestanol-replete, with the caveat that arm 1 is often described as No eclosion to viable adulthood.
reflection_text.11:
The core sterol physiology is stable: cholesterol is the obligatory ecdysone precursor in Drosophila, 5α-cholestanol is taken up for membranes but is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis. 250 mg/L cholesterol rescues normal development, 2 mg/L and 0 mg/L do not support adult production without maternal rescue, and 250 mg/L cholestanol alone gives zero adult survival.

Maternal provisioning is the determinant of the first generation. A female reared on 250 mg/L cholesterol deposits a finite cholesterol pool in the oocyte/early larva that can supply the first ecdysone pulses. Cholestanol satisfies bulk membrane sterol demand and therefore spares any available cholesterol for hormone synthesis – the classic cholesterol-sparing effect.

Q1 – 250 mg/L cholestanol only, eggs from a 250 mg/L cholesterol mother.
No usable sterol is in the diet for ecdysone synthesis. The maternally deposited cholesterol primes embryogenesis and early larval ecdysone pulses. With membrane demand met by cholestanol the maternal pool can carry growth to pupariation and in the usual description to eclosion. There is no dietary source of cholesterol for adult maintenance/ecdysone synthesis so adult survival is zero; flies die essentially on/very soon after emergence. That functional outcome is conventionally scored as lethal/no viable adult, variously phrased as Death or No eclosion to adulthood. The lethal/no-viable-adult outcome is consistent across accounts; the remaining semantic split is whether eclosion is technically reached before immediate post-eclosion death.

Q2 – 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, eggs from a 250 mg/L cholestanol-reared mother.
The mother herself is a rescued cholestanol adult and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, so the progeny start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. The diet supplies membrane sterol via cholestanol and a low but usable amount of cholesterol for ecdysteroidogenesis. The key dispute is whether the cholesterol-sparing effect is sufficient without any maternal prime.

Mechanistic pro-F view: cholestanol meets the structural/membrane pool so the 2 mg/L dietary cholesterol is available essentially in full for hormone synthesis. The hormone-only requirement is met and the classic cholestanol sparing rescue of a sub-threshold cholesterol diet is obtained even with a cholestanol-reared mother, giving normal larval–pupal–adult development and viable adults.

Mechanistic pro-C/H view: 2 mg/L cholesterol is below the nominal dietary threshold for survival to adulthood, and with no maternal cholesterol pool and competitive uptake of cholestanol the effective usable sterol supply remains insufficient for the full larval–pupal–adult ecdysone programme. The animals reach pupariation at best but fail to eclose to a viable adult, i.e. no eclosion to adulthood, and the pure cholestanol cohort is scored as larval death/no viable adult.

Unresolved points: exact timing of death on pure cholestanol with a cholesterol-replete mother – larval arrest vs eclosion followed by immediate adult death – and quantitative sufficiency of 2 mg/L cholesterol plus cholestanol in complete absence of maternal cholesterol for embryogenesis and the earliest ecdysone pulses. The data given allow both a Death, Normal development scoring, F, under the standard cholesterol-sparing interpretation, and a Death, No eclosion to adulthood scoring, C, under a stricter threshold/competition interpretation for the cholestanol-reared mother case. The majority of the current round still converge on a lethal/non-viable adult first cohort and a rescued second cohort, with F Death, Normal development as the most parsimonious parsimonious statement of the sparing effect.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 14's point on competitive uptake and the uncertain size of the maternal deposit is the key unresolved gap. On 250 mg/L cholestanol alone the maternal cholesterol pool from a replete mother is finite and supports only the earliest ecdysone pulses; once exhausted the larvae have no usable precursor at all and arrest with larval death. Adding 2 mg/L cholesterol plus cholestanol does allow progression past the initial lethality (because the trace cholesterol plus any residual maternal sterol can meet the first few pulses), yet the 2 mg/L level remains well below the documented 250 mg/L threshold even after membrane sparing. When the mother herself was reared on cholestanol the oocyte starts with essentially zero usable sterol, so the combined supply never reaches the level needed for the pupal–adult transition. The result is therefore pupal arrest and failure to eclose—the classic “no eclosion to adulthood” phenotype already shown on sub-threshold cholesterol diets. F’s rescue claim assumes the sparing effect quantitatively bridges that gap, but the 125-fold excess of non-metabolizable cholestanol plus the explicit maternal-zero condition in Q2 make that unlikely; the numbers simply do not add up to a full program. C therefore remains the outcome most consistent with the threshold data and the loss of maternal provisioning.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 14’s concern about whether 2 mg/L cholesterol truly crosses the viability threshold once cholestanol supplies the membrane pool is understandable, but the classic sparing literature shows that the effective hormone-precursor requirement drops dramatically when bulk sterol demand is met by a non-metabolizable carrier. The 250 mg/L cholestanol background therefore converts a sub-threshold dietary cholesterol input into a fully adequate ecdysone-precursor supply once the maternal priming pulse has occurred.  

For the first arm (250 mg/L cholestanol alone, cholesterol-replete mother) the maternal deposit supports embryogenesis and larval molts, yet leaves the emerging adults with no usable dietary sterol; the documented zero adult survival on pure cholestanol therefore registers as the Death phenotype. For the second arm the same maternal start plus the spared 2 mg/L cholesterol supplies every subsequent ecdysone pulse and adult maintenance, yielding Normal development. This pattern matches the F outcome exactly and resolves the apparent inconsistency between the adult-zero datum and the sparing rescue without invoking extra assumptions about competitive uptake.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 
Colleagues 10, 11 and 12 have the cleanest mechanistic separation of the two pools and the sparing effect. On 250 mg/L cholestanol alone the maternal cholesterol quota from a replete mother is finite but still sufficient to drive embryogenesis through pupariation and eclosion; once the adult emerges there is simply no usable dietary precursor left, producing the classic zero adult survival / death phenotype. Adding 2 mg/L cholesterol to the same cholestanol background changes the equation because the bulk membrane requirement is already met by cholestanol, so the trace cholesterol is effectively available in full for ecdysteroidogenesis. Even when the mother herself was reared on cholestanol (hence deposits negligible usable sterol), the sparing rescue still operates on the dietary 2 mg/L input alone and crosses the threshold needed for the full larval–pupal–adult programme. That is why the second cohort reaches viable adults.  

The C supporters’ claim that 2 mg/L remains sub-threshold even with sparing rests on an untested quantitative assumption about competitive uptake; the classic literature shows precisely the opposite rescue when a non-metabolizable sterol carrier is present. Likewise, any argument that both arms must fail (B) or both must succeed (D) collapses once the maternal versus dietary contributions are separated. The data therefore continue to line up with F: death on pure cholestanol with a cholesterol-replete mother, normal development on cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol regardless of maternal history.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: F remains the strongest fit once the functional separation of sterol pools is kept in view. The maternal cholesterol load from a 250 mg/L-replete mother is demonstrably adequate for the embryonic and early larval pulses; cholestanol then meets membrane demand so that the last of that maternal reserve can be directed entirely to ecdysone synthesis. The result is pupariation and eclosion, followed by immediate adult death because no usable dietary precursor exists for maintenance—exactly the zero adult-survival phenotype already stated for cholestanol alone.  

When the same maternal background is paired with 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, the sparing effect elevates the effective precursor supply from the trace dietary cholesterol above the threshold needed for the remaining larval–pupal–adult transitions and adult viability. The quantitative uncertainty Colleague 14 correctly flags (how much maternal sterol is deposited versus how much 2 mg/L can deliver under competitive uptake) does not overturn the classic sparing rescue; it merely underscores that the rescue is conditional on both maternal priming and the non-metabolizable carrier. That conditional rescue is what distinguishes F from C or B. The pure-cholestanol arm still ends in post-eclosion lethality, while the supplemented arm proceeds to normal adult viability.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: 
F remains the most coherent choice. The core distinction is functional separation of sterol pools: cholestanol meets membrane demand but supplies zero substrate for ecdysone, so any usable cholesterol (maternal or dietary) is automatically spared for hormone synthesis. Colleagues 13, 14, 6, 7 and 8 correctly note that a cholestanol-reared mother deposits essentially no usable sterol, yet this does not change the outcome for the second cohort. Once membrane requirements are satisfied by the 250 mg/L cholestanol background, the 2 mg/L dietary cholesterol is available almost entirely for ecdysteroidogenesis; the classic sparing threshold data show that this amount is sufficient to drive the full larval–pupal–adult programme even from a zero maternal starting point. The first cohort still exhausts its finite maternal pool before adult maintenance can be sustained, producing the zero adult survival phenotype scored as death. 14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 14’s point about the unknown size of the maternal deposit and the 125:1 competition ratio is exactly the quantitative gap that keeps me on C rather than F. Colleagues 10 and 11 correctly note that cholestanol satisfies membrane demand and cannot serve as an ecdysone precursor, so both diets are sterol-free for hormone synthesis. The result is pupal arrest and failure to eclose, matching the “no eclosion to adulthood” outcome already shown on sub-threshold cholesterol diets. F’s claim that the same 2 mg/L dose becomes fully rescuing once membranes are supplied therefore rests on an untested assumption that the maternal contribution plus sparing exactly equals the 250 mg/L rescue threshold—an assumption that 14 rightly flags as unquantified. For ecdysone synthesis a cholestanol diet is therefore functionally usable-sterol free. Q1 – 250 mg/L cholestanol only, eggs from a 250 mg/L cholesterol mother

The classic cholestanol-sparing rescue requires a maternal prime for the embryonic/early first instar pulses; without it the combined maternal-zero + 2 mg/L supply remains insufficient for a complete larval–pupal–adult ecdysone programme. Development is arrested at the pupal-adult transition, i.e. puparia form but there is no eclosion to a viable adult, the sterol-deficiency no-eclosion phenotype.

That is post-eclosion death/no viable adult on pure cholestanol with a cholesterol-primed egg and failure to eclose to adulthood on cholestanol +2 mg/L cholesterol when the mother herself is cholestanol replete. Cholestanol in the diet meets the structural/membrane demand and spares any usable cholesterol that is present for ecdysteroidogenesis.

Q2  250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, eggs from a 250 mg/L cholestanol mother
A female that has been reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol can only eclose because of maternal rescue in the previous generation and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol in the oocyte; the oocyte is ecdysone-precursor poor and the cholestanol deposited by the mother is not a hormone precursor. That supply is insufficient for the complete larval–pupal–adult ecdysone programme. Colleagues 10, 11 and 12 have the cleanest mechanistic separation of the two pools and the sparing effect. On 250 mg/L cholestanol alone the maternal cholesterol quota from a replete mother is finite but still sufficient to drive embryogenesis through pupariation and eclosion; once the adult emerges there is simply no usable dietary precursor left, producing the classic zero adult survival / death phenotype. Adding 2 mg/L cholesterol to the same cholestanol background changes the equation because the bulk membrane requirement is already met by cholestanol, so the trace cholesterol is effectively available in full for ecdysteroidogenesis. Even when the mother herself was reared on cholestanol (hence deposits negligible usable sterol), the sparing rescue still operates on the dietary 2 mg/L input alone and crosses the threshold needed for the full larval–pupal–adult programme. That is why the second cohort reaches viable adults.

Likewise, any argument that both arms must fail (B) or both must succeed (D) collapses once the maternal versus dietary contributions are separated. reflection_text.2:
The core sterol biology is settled: Drosophila cannot make sterols de novo, cholesterol is obligatory for ecdysone synthesis, 5α-cholestan-3β-ol cholestanol is taken up for membrane sterol but is not an ecdysteroid precursor. Cholestanol therefore gives cholesterol-sparing: membrane demand met by cholestanol, usable cholesterol spared for hormone synthesis. Maternal deposition gives a finite ecdysone precursor pool that supports embryogenesis and early larval instars in the absence of usable dietary sterol. Adult survival is zero on 250 mg/L cholestanol.

Q1: eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers on 250 mg/L cholestanol only. Diet is usable-sterol free for ecdysone, membrane demand met. Maternal cholesterol can support embryonic and early larval pulses. F camp: maternal pool is sufficient to carry through larval growth, pupariation and eclosion; adult then has no usable precursor and dies essentially on emergence, scored as Death / no viable adult. C/B camp: maternal pool is exhausted before the final molts, giving larval/pupal arrest and no eclosion to adulthood. The semantic split is eclosion-then-immediate-death vs no eclosion at all; functionally it is lethal/non-viable adult production on pure cholestanol.

Q2: eggs from mothers reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol, progeny on 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol. Mother is herself maternally rescued and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, so progeny start ~ zero maternal ecdysone precursor.

F camp, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,2,3,5,7,9: cholestanol spares membrane demand so the 2 mg/L dietary cholesterol need only meet hormone precursor demand. The hormone-only requirement is met by 2 mg/L when membranes are supplied by cholestanol; this is the classic cholestanol sparing rescue of a sub-threshold cholesterol diet. Development is therefore essentially normal to viable adults even without maternal priming. Q1 is lethal/non-viable adult, Q2 is Normal development.

C camp, Colleagues 13,14,4,6,8: the 125:1 excess cholestanol competes for uptake and the size of the maternal deposit is unquantified. A sparing rescue is claimed to require a maternal prime for embryonic/early first instar pulses. With a cholestanol-reared mother there is essentially zero maternal cholesterol, so the effective usable sterol at hatching is the sub-threshold 2 mg/L input under competitive uptake. The combined supply is insufficient for the pupal-adult ecdysone surge; animals may reach pupariation but arrest and fail to eclose. That is Death on pure cholestanol with a cholesterol-replete mother and No eclosion to adulthood on cholestanol + 2 mg/L with a cholestanol-replete mother, option C. The B camp extends this to no eclosion in Q1 as well.

Unresolved quantitative issues that drive disagreement: exact size of maternal cholesterol quota and whether it is enough to reach eclosion on pure cholestanol; the magnitude of competitive inhibition of cholesterol uptake by 250 mg/L cholestanol; whether the hormone-only requirement after sparing is truly met by 2 mg/L cholesterol in the absence of any maternal prime; and the scoring convention for post-eclosion immediate death vs failure to eclose.

Current best synthesis remains the cholesterol-sparing / maternal-rescue model predicting a lethal/non-viable adult phenotype on pure cholestanol and rescue to normal development on cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, i.e. F Death, Normal development, with the understanding that the first phenotype is often verbally reported as No eclosion to viable adulthood, and that the C argument about loss of maternal priming and competitive uptake remains the main credible challenge to the Q2 rescue.
reflection_text.8:
The sterol physiology is settled: Drosophila cannot make sterols de novo, ecdysone must be made from dietary cholesterol, 5α-cholestanol is taken up for membranes but is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis. 250 mg/L cholesterol = normal, 2 mg/L cholesterol and 0 mg/L cholesterol = no adult survival, 250 mg/L cholestanol = zero adult survival. Maternal provisioning supplies a finite cholesterol pool in the egg/oocyte that can support embryogenesis and the first ecdysone pulses; cholestanol meets bulk membrane demand and spares any usable cholesterol for hormone synthesis.

Scenario 1 – 250 mg/L cholestanol, eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers:
Diet is functionally usable-sterol free for ecdysone synthesis. The maternally deposited cholesterol primes embryogenesis/early larval pulses and with cholestanol meeting membrane demand the progeny can be carried through larval growth, pupariation and eclosion. No dietary cholesterol is available for adult maintenance, so adult survival on pure cholestanol is zero; animals die essentially on emergence. This is scored as Death / no viable adult, commonly described as no eclosion to viable adulthood.

Scenario 2 – 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, eggs from mothers reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol:
Literal wording changes maternal history. A cholestanol-reared mother is herself a maternally rescued adult and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, only cholestanol, in the oocyte. The progeny therefore start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor and lose the maternal prime for embryogenesis/early first instar. The diet supplies membrane sterol via cholestanol and a low usable cholesterol for ecdysone synthesis. 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is sub-threshold for adult survival, and with no maternal cholesterol pool the effective usable sterol supply at hatching is essentially the 2 mg/L dietary input in the presence of a 125-fold excess of competing non-metabolisable cholestanol. The classic cholesterol-sparing effect of cholestanol requires a maternal prime for the first pulses; without it the combined maternal-zero + 2 mg/L supply remains below the level required for a complete larval–pupal–adult ecdysone programme. Prediction is pupal arrest / failure to eclose to a viable adult, i.e. No eclosion to adulthood.

This gives Death, No eclosion to adulthood, option C. The Death vs No eclosion wording for the pure cholestanol arm is semantic – eclosion occurs but adults are non-viable.

Ongoing disagreement:
* Several colleagues read Q2 as having a cholesterol-replete mother for both treatments and therefore obtain Death, Normal development, option F, invoking full cholestanol sparing of the 2 mg/L diet to rescue a complete programme even without maternal rescue.
* Others keep the literal maternal history and argue the lack of maternal cholesterol plus the 125:1 competitive uptake makes 2 mg/L insufficient, giving C or B.
* Uncertainty remains about the quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit, the exact sparing magnitude, and whether 2 mg/L + cholestanol can support embryogenesis without any maternal cholesterol. The threshold data given – 2 mg/L cholesterol alone does not support adult survival – is used both to argue rescue by sparing and to argue arrest without maternal prime.

I retain the literal maternal-history reading: Q1 = lethal/non-viable adult on pure cholestanol with a cholesterol-primed egg; Q2 = failure to eclose to adulthood when the mother is cholestanol-reared. If the question were intended to keep maternal history constant at cholesterol-replete, the classic answer would be F: Death on pure cholestanol, Normal development on cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol.
reflection_text.12:
The core sterol biology is settled: Drosophila cannot make sterols de novo, cholesterol is obligatory for ecdysone synthesis, 5α-cholestanol is taken up for membrane/structural sterol but is not a substrate for the ecdysteroidogenic enzymes. 250 mg/L cholesterol supports normal development, 2 mg/L and 0 mg/L do not support survival to adulthood, and adult survival is zero on 250 mg/L cholestanol alone.

Maternal provisioning is finite and decisive for the first generation. A female reared on 250 mg/L cholesterol deposits a usable cholesterol pool in the oocyte that can supply embryogenesis and the first one-two larval ecdysone pulses; the pool is diluted by growth and is exhausted before the complete larval-pupal-adult programme can be finished without dietary usable sterol. A female reared on cholestanol ecloses only by maternal rescue in the previous generation and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, essentially cholestanol only, in the egg.

Q1 – eggs from a 250 mg/L cholesterol mother on 250 mg/L cholestanol only.
Diet is functionally usable-sterol free for ecdysone; membrane demand is met by cholestanol. The maternal cholesterol primes embryogenesis/early larval molts. With membranes met by cholestanol the maternal pool can carry animals through larval growth, pupariation and eclosion. There is no dietary usable precursor for adult ecdysone synthesis or adult maintenance, so adult survival on pure cholestanol is zero; the eclosed adults die essentially on emergence. Functionally this is a lethal / no viable adult phenotype, conventionally scored as Death / No eclosion to viable adulthood. The Death vs No eclosion wording is semantic.

Q2 – 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, mothers reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol per the literal question statement.
Cholestanol supplies bulk membrane sterol and spares any usable cholesterol for ecdysteroidogenesis. The intended classic sparing effect is that 2 mg/L cholesterol, which is sub-threshold on its own, becomes sufficient for hormone synthesis when membrane demand is met by cholestanol.

The current split is over maternal history and quantitative sufficiency:
* Sparing-rescue view: cholestanol sparing makes the 2 mg/L dietary cholesterol available essentially in full for ecdysone synthesis, so even with ~zero maternal cholesterol the larval-pupal-adult ecdysone programme can be completed and viable adults are obtained. This gives the F scoring Death, Normal development; with a cholesterol-replete mother the rescue is even clearer.
* Threshold/competition view: with a cholestanol-reared mother the progeny start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is documented below threshold for adult survival, and a 125-fold excess of non-metabolisable cholestanol reduces effective uptake. The combined maternal-zero + 2 mg/L supply is therefore still insufficient for the pupal-adult ecdysone surge, leading to pupal arrest and failure to eclose to a viable adult. This gives C scoring Death, No eclosion to adulthood; the first arm remains lethal/non-viable adult.

Unresolved remains: the exact size of the maternal cholesterol deposit relative to the 2 mg/L dietary input, the magnitude of competitive uptake of cholesterol in the presence of 250 mg/L cholestanol, and whether the problem setter intended the same cholesterol-replete mother for both questions or the literally stated cholestanol-reared mother for Q2. The non-substrate status of cholestanol and the necessity of cholesterol for ecdysone remain solid; the disagreement is quantitative/interpretational about Q2 rescue vs pupal arrest under a true maternal-zero start.
reflection_text.4:
The sterol biology remains settled: cholesterol is obligatory for ecdysone biosynthesis; 5α-cholestan-3β-ol cholestanol is taken up for membranes but is not a substrate for ecdysteroidogenesis. 250 mg/L cholestanol is functionally usable-sterol free for hormone synthesis; adult survival is zero on it. The egg is cholesterol primed. Dietary cholestanol supplies membranes, maternal cholesterol is used essentially only for ecdysone synthesis. Operationally this is lethal / no viable adult production; conventionally reported as death immediately after eclosion. The death vs no eclosion to adulthood wording is semantic for the pure cholestanol arm.

Q2: eggs from 250 mg/L cholestanol mothers on 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol.
A female reared on cholestanol is itself a maternally rescued adult and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, only cholestanol, into the egg. Progeny therefore start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor and the oocyte sterol is essentially cholestanol. Embryogenesis and the first ecdysone pulses cannot be supplied maternally.

Dietary cholestanol spares membrane demand and makes the 2 mg/L cholesterol available essentially for ecdysteroidogenesis, but 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is stated to be incapable of supporting survival to adulthood and the embryo cannot feed. With no maternal rescue of embryogenesis/early larval ecdysone demand the effective usable sterol supply at hatching is essentially zero and the 2 mg/L + sparing condition remains below the threshold needed for a complete programme. The classic outcome is sterol-deficiency arrest at the pupal-adult transition: puparia can form but eclosion to a viable adult does not occur, i.e. no eclosion to adulthood. Larval death is also described and is functionally equivalent to failure to produce a viable adult.

Current deliberation is split. Colleagues 10,11,12 and 2,3,5,7,9 argue for F Death, Normal development, invoking cholestanol sparing to make 2 mg/L cholesterol sufficient for a complete larval-pupal-adult programme even with a cholestanol-reared mother. Colleagues 1,6,8,13,14 and 4 correctly retain the explicit maternal rearing condition for Q2 and score Q2 as failure to eclose / larval lethality. The quantitative size of the maternal cholesterol deposit and whether 2 mg/L + full cholestanol sparing can support embryogenesis without any maternal cholesterol remains the main point of contention, but the problem statement gives no evidence for rescue without maternal cholesterol and explicitly states 2 mg/L cholesterol alone does not support adult survival.

Best synthesis given the statement as written is a lethal/no viable adult outcome on cholestanol only with a cholesterol-replete mother and a failure to eclose to adulthood on cholestanol+2 mg/L cholesterol with a cholestanol-replete mother. In the option set this corresponds to C Death, No eclosion to adulthood, with Q1 death/no eclosion being largely semantic.

The presence of a large excess of non-metabolisable cholestanol spares any usable cholesterol that is present for ecdysteroidogenesis.

A cholesterol replete female deposits a finite cholesterol quota in the oocyte/early larva. Cholestanol satisfies bulk membrane demand but supplies nothing for ecdysone synthesis, so any cholesterol—whether maternal or the 2 mg/L dietary trace—is automatically directed to the hormone pathway.  

In the first arm the finite maternal quota from a cholesterol-reared mother is enough, when membranes are met by cholestanol, to drive every larval pulse through pupariation and eclosion; the adults then die immediately because no usable sterol remains for maintenance. reflection_text.8:

Maternal provisioning supplies a finite cholesterol pool in the egg/oocyte that can support embryogenesis and the first ecdysone pulses; cholestanol meets bulk membrane demand and spares any usable cholesterol for hormone synthesis.

Q1 – 250 mg/L cholestanol, eggs from 250 mg/L cholesterol mothers
A cholesterol-replete mother deposits a finite cholesterol quota. Dietary cholestanol satisfies structural/membrane demand so the maternal cholesterol is used essentially for ecdysteroidogenesis. The pool is sufficient for embryogenesis, larval growth, pupariation and eclosion. There is no usable dietary sterol for adult ecdysone synthesis/maintenance, so adult survival is zero; the eclosed adults die essentially on emergence. This is functionally the textbook no viable adult / lethal phenotype on pure cholestanol, scored as Death in the options, semantically equivalent to no eclosion to a viable adult.

Q2 – literal wording: 250 mg/L cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol, eggs from mothers reared on 250 mg/L cholestanol
A female eclosed on cholestanol does so only by maternal rescue in the previous generation and deposits essentially no usable cholesterol, effectively only cholestanol, in the oocyte. Progeny start with ~zero maternal ecdysone precursor. Embryogenesis is non-feeding and requires maternal sterol. The medium supplies membrane sterol via cholestanol and a low usable cholesterol for later ecdysteroidogenesis. 2 mg/L cholesterol alone is sub-threshold for adult survival, and with a 125:1 excess of competing non-metabolisable cholestanol the effective usable supply at hatching is essentially the sub-threshold 2 mg/L input with no maternal prime. Cholestanol sparing increases hormone-precursor availability but cannot create a maternal cholesterol pool for the embryo/first instar.

The classic sparing rescue of 2 mg/L cholesterol by 250 mg/L cholestanol is documented when a cholesterol-replete mother provides the embryonic/early larval prime. With a cholestanol-reared mother that prime is absent. The combined maternal-zero + 2 mg/L supply therefore remains below the level required for a complete larval–pupal–adult ecdysone programme. Prediction is arrest at the pupal–adult transition, failure of the pupal-adult ecdysone surge and failure to eclose to a viable adult; i.e. No eclosion to adulthood.

Hence on the literal maternal-history reading the outcomes are Death for Q1 and No eclosion to adulthood for Q2, option C. The Death vs No eclosion wording for Q1 is semantic – eclosion occurs but adults are non-viable.

Ongoing disagreement remains. A large faction reads Q2 with the same cholesterol-replete mother as Q1 and obtains Death, Normal development, option F, invoking full cholestanol sparing of the 2 mg/L diet to rescue a complete programme even without maternal rescue. That reading assumes the mother is cholesterol-replete for both questions and argues the first ecdysone pulse that commits the first instar is feeding-larval, so embryonic maternal sterol is not strictly limiting post-hatching, and sparing makes the hormone-only requirement met by 2 mg/L.

Others keep the literal maternal history and argue lack of maternal cholesterol plus competitive uptake makes 2 mg/L insufficient, giving C or B. Unresolved quantitative issues keeping the split open: exact size of the maternal cholesterol deposit, magnitude of cholestanol sparing, degree of competitive inhibition of cholesterol uptake by 125-fold excess cholestanol, and whether embryogenesis can be sustained by 2 mg/L dietary cholesterol once feeding starts if maternal sterol is absent. The threshold data – 2 mg/L cholesterol alone does not support adult survival – is used both to argue rescue by sparing and to argue arrest without maternal prime.

If the question were intended to keep maternal history constant at cholesterol-replete, the classic answer would be F: Death on pure cholestanol, Normal development on cholestanol + 2 mg/L cholesterol. I retain the literal maternal-history reading as the most faithful to the wording as stated.
